findings.now: It was the result of years of work, traveling to all kinds of communes and communal experiments around the country, trying to answer a question that for him was primary: How do we live together without recreating the same loneliness, domination, and stupidity we were supposedly escaping?
At the time that meant a lot of boredom, with some adventures mixed in, but those years gave me a great sample to compare against.
In case you aren’t familiar with Y2K, it was the Year 2000 (represented as year 00) computer bug which some folks like my dad especially, felt might be the end of civilization.
At Love Israel, I had my dream of picking all kinds of wild berries in nature come true.

There were like eight people at Acorn when I was there, and no kids. I couldn’t tell whether it was a commune I might join or a group of people who were already friends, and who happened to live on some really beautiful land and be good at building cool stuff.
It was more like a tiny hippie town, but with a highly structured political system that didn’t seem intuitive for hippies.
Suddenly, the longing to escape loneliness which inspired my father’s movie, is everywhere again.

Back in 2023, ironically, just the year after Covid lockdowns ended, the U.S. Surgeon General even put out an advisory, saying roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a **public-health** issue.
In a large society the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart, and that’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths.
Apart from the Covid lockdowns just prior, AI became serious around this time, and it started changing people’s jobs and relationships, and how they see the future.

Later, when another influencer with a big following floated the commune idea, the comment section started to become a recruitment board, where people were apparently forming joint operations together right in there.

Some of the commenters were skeptics tho. The oldest objection showed up immediately, restating the collective action problem: anarcho-communalism sounds great on paper, but when property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” the practicality comes into question.
Any attempt at communal ownership needs to take this into account by having folks take on visible and named stewardship duties, and by having a plan to deal with leeches.
No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish, thieving, nor suddenly unlearning learned helplessness.
The How-To Manual after this essay deals with these issues.
Most communes of my acquaintance traded inner freedom of the heart (spirituality) for outer freedom (secular, nondogmatic, political). The two pendulum ends of this trade-off mirror each other.
A place where people who’ve done the healing first can join without pretending they’re fully finished, and that also has peer practice and enough play that it doesn’t become a permanent repair shop.
Each of us guides our own compatible practice, and our practices weave the community into the quilt that keeps us all warm and safe.
Secular communities, on the other hand, often call it “the process,” which can become just as sacred.
Uh, but wait, where do you find these people?
Fun and nice things first give incentive.
And once you’re past those phases, if you still want to live together, you can all meet in a rented or borrowed space, or at each other’s houses, long before anyone needs a land surveyor.

And I believe there are real reasons to take psychedelics communally too - e.g. they can lower defensive barriers which otherwise dominate every serious conversation, and create strong bonds between members of the community who have been through the harder nights together.
After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at age 25, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar.

Do you trust the people you’re relying on for support?** Support from people you trust is different from paid support, which is often paying people you don’t know to look after you for a night. To me it seems way too much of a gamble if I have a better alternative.
Is your community humble enough to say no? To pause? Using the medicine takes that.

That answers the reasonable objection that communes are just privileged escape pods, which gets double dipped with the objection that psychedelics are also privileged escape pods (or, alternatively, as some say, “a vacation for the poor”).

ZEGG, a community near Berlin, and Tamera, a ZEGG offshoot in Portugal, have spent decades experimenting with relationships inside community. They are an example of how a community can acknowledge the erotic aspects of life.
I feel very much saddened by the way that adults are seen as (and actually often are) so dangerous for children in the West, especially when they are fond of each other.

Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community.** Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. There was apparently some physical abuse going on there as a disciplinary practice, but that’s something which varies a lot in every society also.
In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, hopefully including non-intrusive help from outside the home community.
What kind of legal or illegal entity (cooperative, trust, association, company, or tribal squatting?) will hold the land? This needs to be decided before it’s bought or occupied.
Read the founderism questions next, and agree on the exit terms in “Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution” before anyone commits.
Members might have outside jobs, and they bring an agreed share of that income in.

Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who’s in charge of the resources? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the people who review the founder? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart mi
If several are present, they are worth paying attention to before the founder(s) can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way.
While founderism is a problem in every community, it’s especially so in communities which form naturally over time as I’m describing may happen in my case.
But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain.
But some practices go too far against the communal spirit.
Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm.

Dissent is important for growth. Sometimes it really is their wounded ego projection, and that should be acknowledged. But again, balance, because if complaints are too often or too broadly painted as projection, that’s as much a failure, if not more so.

There are some basic human rights that can’t be voted away from you by the majority in a community, unless it’s a question of resource availability as a whole. If safety and the conditions for health can be provided, they should be provided. People should be able to maintain relationships with other

Decide in advance which offers of help are purely goodwill and which go on a ledger of mutual aid. The federation can keep track of these for each purpose, without having to put a value on them or require every exchange to be “even”.

makes an uncomfortable argument: the communities that last a long time often rely on a religious ideology which makes members feel alienated from the wider society. Basically, the more cultish, the more durable, since cults are designed to capture people.
